questions.question_text:
The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through $(3, 5)$ and the graph of $y = g(x)$ has an $x$-intercept at $(3, 0)$.
What point must lie on the sum graph $y = f(x) + g(x)$?

options.why: Kept the correct $x$-value but added the $x$-value $3$ to the ordinate $5$ instead of adding $g(3) = 0$, giving $5 + 3 = 8$.
Added the two points coordinate by coordinate, so the $x$-coordinates were added as well: $3 + 3 = 6$, while the ordinate stayed $5 + 0 = 5$.
Made both slips at once: added the $x$-coordinates ($3 + 3 = 6$) and also added the $x$-value $3$ to the ordinate ($5 + 3 = 8$).

questions.question_text:
The curves $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ intersect at $(2, -3)$ and $(-1, 4)$.
What are the corresponding points on the graph of $y = f(x) + g(x)$?

options.why: Assumed the sum graph simply passes through the intersection points, forgetting to double the equal ordinates.
Doubled the $x$-coordinates as well as the ordinates, treating the sum as a dilation of the whole point.
Doubled the $x$-coordinates instead of the ordinates, leaving the $y$-values of the intersection points unchanged.

questions.solution_text:
At an intersection point where $f(x) = g(x) = k$, the sum is $f(x) + g(x) = 2k$.
At $x = 2$: $y = -3 + (-3) = -6 \implies (2, -6)$.
At $x = -1$: $y = 4 + 4 = 8 \implies (-1, 8)$.
$(2, -6)$ and $(-1, 8)$

questions.question_text:
The graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ intersect at $x = -2$ and $x = 5$.
At which points does the graph of $y = f(x) - g(x)$ cut the $x$-axis?

options.why: Swapped the $x$ and $y$ coordinate positions.
Negated the $x$-intercept values.
Combined the intersection $x$-values rather than identifying each individual zero.

questions.solution_text:
$d(x) = f(x) - g(x) = 0 \iff f(x) = g(x)$.
Since the graphs intersect at $x = -2$ and $x = 5$, $d(-2) = 0$ and $d(5) = 0$.
$(-2, 0)$ and $(5, 0)$

questions.question_text: Which line is an asymptote of the curve $y = 2x + 3^{-x}$ as $x \to \infty$?

options.why: Confused the horizontal asymptote of $3^{-x}$ with the asymptote of the combined sum.
Treated the base $3$ as a constant vertical shift.
Mistook the $y$-axis for a vertical asymptote.

questions.question_text: What are the vertical asymptotes of the sum function $y = \dfrac{2}{x-1} + \dfrac{3}{x+4}$?

options.why: Read the roots straight off the denominators without changing sign, giving $-1$ from $x - 1$ and $4$ from $x + 4$.
Solved the denominators correctly but wrote the lines as $y = c$, confusing vertical lines with horizontal ones.
Made both slips: took the denominator constants without changing sign and then wrote them as horizontal lines $y = c$.

questions.solution_text:
Vertical asymptotes occur where either denominator is zero.
$x - 1 = 0 \implies x = 1$
$x + 4 = 0 \implies x = -4$
$x = 1$ and $x = -4$

questions.question_text: For the function $y = |x - 5| + |x + 2|$, what is the constant value of $y$ on the interval $[-2, 5]$?

options.why: Subtracted the boundary values $5 - 2 = 3$ instead of adding the distances.
Doubled the larger endpoint value.
Assumed the two absolute value terms cancel to zero between the roots.

questions.question_text: If $f(x)$ is an even function and $g(x)$ is an even function, which statement best describes the parity of $d(x) = f(x) - g(x)$ and gives the correct reason?

options.text: $d(x)$ is always even, because $d(-x) = f(-x) - g(-x) = f(x) - g(x) = d(x)$.
$d(x)$ is always odd, because subtracting two symmetric functions inverts their parity.
options.why: Assumed subtraction converts even symmetry into odd symmetry.

options.text: $d(x)$ has no symmetry in general, because subtraction destroys symmetry.
options.why: Assumed the difference of two functions always loses symmetry.

options.text: $d(x)$ is identically zero for any two even functions.
options.why: Assumed two even functions must be identical.

questions.solution_text:
Since $f$ and $g$ are even, $f(-x) = f(x)$ and $g(-x) = g(x)$.
$d(-x) = f(-x) - g(-x) = f(x) - g(x) = d(x)$.
Since $d(-x) = d(x)$, $d(x)$ is **even**.

questions.question_text:
Let $f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2$ and $g(x) = 3x^3 - x$.
Which statement correctly describes the parity of $s(x) = f(x) + g(x)$ and gives the correct algebraic justification?

options.text: $s(x)$ is neither even nor odd because $s(-x) \neq s(x)$ and $s(-x) \neq -s(x)$.
$s(x)$ is strictly even because the highest degree term $x^4$ determines polynomial parity.
options.why: Ignored the odd polynomial component $g(x)$.

options.text: $s(x)$ is strictly odd because the linear and cubic terms dominate the behaviour.
options.why: Ignored the even polynomial component $f(x)$.

options.text: $s(x)$ is symmetric about the vertical line $x = 1$.
options.why: Confused point and line symmetry properties.

questions.solution_text:
$s(x) = x^4 + 3x^3 - 2x^2 - x$
$s(-x) = x^4 - 3x^3 - 2x^2 + x$
$-s(x) = -x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x^2 + x$
Since $s(-x) \neq s(x)$ and $s(-x) \neq -s(x)$, $s(x)$ is **neither even nor odd**.
